item.title: What C Actually Does With Your Struct - Padding, Alignment and Memory Layout
item.author: Alessandro Miragliotta
item.description: Many computer systems put alignment restrictions to simplify the design of the hardware between the processor and the memory. Such restrictions require that the address for some objects must be a multiple of some value V (typically 2,4, or 8). For example, suppose a processor always fetches 8 bytes from memory with an address that must be a multiple of 8. If we can guarantee that any double will be aligned to have its address be a multiple of 8, then the value can be read or written with a single memory operation. Otherwise, we may need to perform two memory accesses, since the object might be split across two 8-byte memory blocks and that impacts performances.
